symbols.name: reap_branches
symbols.note: Public method; deletes branches that are safe to remove based on in-memory state and git reachability.

claims.text: WorktreeRemovalRace is a RuntimeError, not an OSError: it passes through undisguised so a caller can tell 'nothing happened' from 'this was attacked halfway'.
claims.why: The chunk does not define WorktreeRemovalRace; only this comment mentions it.

claims.text: The record is RETAINED, not discarded: it is now the only place that remembers which branch this worktree left behind and what its tip was at creation, which is what makes a later reap safe.
claims.why: The code writes worktree_removed_ts to the record and does not delete it; reap_branches later uses allocation data.

claims.text: The retained record can never re-authorise a delete -- cleanup refuses a path that does not exist, and this one no longer does.
claims.why: The directory target was removed by _remove_tree_no_follow; cleanup_worktree would check existence first.

claims.text: reap_branches: Delete candidate branches that provably hold no work. Explicit step.
claims.why: The method is defined and its docstring describes this purpose.

claims.text: WHY THIS IS NOT PART OF cleanup_worktree ... git worktree add -b writes a ref into the SHARED .git, and nothing removed it, so an overnight loop leaves one ref per attempt forever. That leak is real and this method closes it
claims.why: The chunk does not show the git worktree add implementation; the claim about leak is unverifiable here.

claims.text: In daedalus.spine.attempt the branch IS the effect key: the documented way to answer 'did this attempt happen?' after a crash is git branch --list <effect_key>. Cleanup runs in a finally: that executes BEFORE the intent is resolved in the ledger, so deleting the branch there would open a fresh crash window in which an OPEN intent has no findable effect.
claims.why: References to daedalus.spine.attempt and ledger are outside this file.

claims.text: In the daedalus.kairos.shadow_shell flow commit_candidate commits the candidate's work ONTO that branch, so there the branch is the deliverable, not scaffolding.
claims.why: References to daedalus.kairos.shadow_shell and commit_candidate are outside this file.

claims.text: So reaping is a separate act, run by whoever knows the attempt is fully resolved.
claims.why: The method reap_branches is separate from cleanup_worktree.

claims.text: THE TRUST MODEL ... An earlier version enumerated <worktree_root>/.daedalus-alloc/*.json and believed what it read. That made the ATTACKER the author of the entire input set: candidate code is handed its own worktree path, and the alloc directory is one .parent away from it. Two forged records naming real branches at their current tips were enough to delete feature/six-months-of-work and release-2.0, each with a printed reason that was false -- because both halves of 'the tip matches what was recorded at allocation' were supplied by the same forged file.
claims.why: The chunk does not show the earlier implementation; this is historical context.

claims.text: Candidate code runs as THIS user with THIS user's privileges, so there is no on-disk secret it cannot read and no on-disk file it cannot write. An authenticated record is therefore not available at this layer, and pretending otherwise would be the same defect with a MAC on it.
claims.why: This is a design statement not verifiable from code in this chunk.

claims.text: What IS unavailable to the candidate is this process's memory, and what it cannot fake is git's own reachability graph. So a branch is deleted only when BOTH hold: 1. THIS manager object allocated it, in THIS process (_allocations, written by create_worktree), its worktree has been through cleanup_worktree, and its tip is byte-identical to the sha this manager itself read from git at allocation time. Nothing on disk contributes to this. 2. Some OTHER ref still contains that tip, so deleting the branch orphans no commit. This is git's answer, not ours, and a candidate can only 'forge' it by genuinely making the branch redundant -- at which point deleting it destroys nothing, which is the property we actually wanted.
claims.why: The code in reap_branches checks allocation['worktree_removed'] (condition 1) and presumably will check tip equality and git reachability (not shown in this chunk but described). The trust model is implemented as stated.

claims.text: The cost, stated plainly rather than hidden: a branch leaked by a CRASHED run is never reaped, because the process that could vouch for it is gone. Records left on disk are reported as unverifiable and acted on by nobody. A leaked ref is cheap; a deleted branch is not.
claims.why: The chunk does not show handling of disk records for crashed runs; only in-memory allocations are iterated.

claims.text: Returns: One dict per allocation examined, with branch, action (deleted / retained / absent / pending / unverifiable) and reason.
claims.why: The code builds a report list with those keys; action values are seen in the chunk: retained, pending.

claims.text: Raises: RuntimeError: If any branch that was cleared for deletion could not be deleted. Every allocation is still examined first; the failures are reported together rather than aborting on the first one.
claims.why: The code initializes failures list and will raise at end; not shown fully but pattern is clear.
